opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important strategic questions in robotics right now, and honestly, I don't see it as a strict either-or, though the two paths do pull you in different directions.

If you focus purely on near-term deployment, you can build something that works today. You pick a narrow task, a structured environment, maybe a warehouse or a factory line, and you engineer the system very carefully: specialized hardware, hand-tuned perception, a lot of task-specific tricks. That can create real value and real revenue. The risk is that every new task becomes a new engineering project. You don't get compounding returns, and when a more general approach matures, a lot of that work may become obsolete. We've seen this pattern in other fields. In natural language processing, many carefully engineered pipelines were swept away once large general models arrived.

On the other hand, if you only chase the "final model," a general-purpose robot foundation model that can do almost anything, you're making a long-term bet. The upside is enormous, but you can spend years without touching the real world in a meaningful way. Robotics is especially unforgiving here, because the real world is messy and the long tail of failure cases is huge. If you never deploy, you never see that long tail, and you never collect the data you need.

So the way I think about it is that deployment should serve the path toward the general model. The most valuable deployments are the ones that generate data and feedback that make the general model better, rather than one-off solutions. Data is the biggest bottleneck in robotics. We don't have an internet-scale corpus of robot actions the way we have text or images. One of the best ways to build that is to get robots out into the world doing useful things, even imperfectly, so they collect experience at scale. That creates a flywheel: deployment produces data, data improves the model, and a better model unlocks more deployment.

The key discipline is resisting the temptation to over-engineer for a single use case. When we build something for a near-term application, I always ask: is this making the general system smarter, or is it a dead end that only works here? If it's the latter, we should be careful about how much we invest in it.

And personally, as a researcher, I'm motivated by the long-term vision. I believe general-purpose embodied intelligence is achievable, and probably sooner than many people expected a few years ago, given how quickly vision-language models and robot learning are converging. But I also think the people who reach that goal will be the ones who stay grounded in the real world along the way. You can't solve robotics entirely in a lab or in simulation. At some point, the robot has to go out and meet reality.

r001.rationale: The response says near-term deployment can create value and revenue, but does not explain that a startup’s need to survive financially limits its ability to focus exclusively on a distant final model.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes a flywheel in which deployment produces data, data improves the model, and a better model enables more deployment toward general-purpose robotics.

r003.rationale: The response says the choice is not a strict either-or and that deployment should serve the general model, but does not state that the two paths ultimately converge on the same solution.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about almost every day, and honestly I don't think it's a clean either-or.

Let me start with the final model. If you look at what happened in language, the lesson is that a single general model trained on enough diverse data eventually beats a thousand narrow systems. I believe the same thing will happen in robotics. There will be a foundation model that takes in vision, language, proprioception, maybe touch, and outputs actions across many robot bodies and many tasks. That's the thing worth building. If you only optimize for the next deployment, you end up with a pile of task-specific pipelines that don't compound, and in five years you've built nothing that transfers.

But here's the problem. Robotics doesn't have an internet of actions. The data isn't sitting there waiting to be scraped. The only way to get large volumes of real-world interaction data is to have robots actually out there doing things, in homes, in warehouses, in hospitals. And nobody pays for a robot that doesn't do something useful today. So deployment isn't a distraction from the final model. It is the data engine for the final model. The companies that get robots into the world first will be the ones with the flywheel.

So the way I think about it is: what you deploy near-term should be chosen so that it feeds the long-term goal. Pick tasks that are commercially valuable enough to justify putting robots in the field, but also diverse enough that the data pushes you toward generality. Avoid the trap of a task so narrow that you can solve it with a hard-coded controller, because then the data you collect teaches the model nothing.

There's one more thing I'd add, which is about simulation and other data sources. Deployment alone won't close the gap fast enough. Simulation, human video, teleoperation, all of those are ways to buy scale while the real-world fleet is still small. The final model will be trained on all of it. But real deployment is the only thing that keeps you honest, because simulation always lies a little, and you don't find out where until a robot drops a cup in someone's kitchen.

So my answer is: aim at the final model, but let near-term deployment set the curriculum. If you do it right, every deployment makes the general model better, and every improvement in the general model opens up the next deployment. If you find yourself choosing between them, it usually means you picked the wrong deployment.

r001.rationale: The response says robots must do something useful today because nobody will pay for them otherwise, and recommends commercially valuable deployments. This communicates the financial pressure that limits a company’s ability to focus only on the distant model.

r002.rationale: It explicitly calls deployment the data engine for the final model and says companies can build a flywheel by getting robots into the world.

r003.rationale: It says each deployment improves the general model and each model improvement enables the next deployment, presenting them as mutually reinforcing paths toward the same goal.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think these are two separate paths. We want to build models that can eventually handle a wide range of tasks, but near-term deployment is how we learn what those models actually need to do.

In robotics, a demo can look very impressive, but deployment exposes a different set of problems: reliability, safety, recovery from mistakes, and the cost of human intervention. Those problems should inform the research. And when robots do useful work, you get experience and data that can help improve the next generation of models.

The tension is that you can spend all your time engineering a solution for one very specific task. That may create value, but it doesn’t necessarily move you toward a more general capability. So I would choose deployments where solving the practical problem also teaches us something that transfers to other tasks.

For me, the long-term goal sets the direction, and deployment gives us a way to test whether we’re making meaningful progress.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a startup’s financial survival needs or how they limit focus on a distant model.

r002.rationale: It says deployment produces experience and data that can improve the next generation of models, linking near-term work to the longer-term goal.

r003.rationale: It calls the paths complementary, but does not state that pursuing the final model directly and making progress through deployments may ultimately converge on the same solution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those two directions should reinforce each other. You need a long-term vision of a model that can handle many different tasks and environments, but you also need to put robots into the real world and learn where they fail.

For near-term deployment, I would choose a problem where the robot can provide clear value and where we can make the system reliable. The important question is whether solving that problem also helps us build more general capabilities. Are we learning something reusable? Are we improving how we collect data, train policies, and evaluate safety?

So I wouldn’t wait for the final model before deploying, and I wouldn’t assume that scaling a collection of narrow solutions will automatically get us there. I’d use the long-term goal to guide the research, and deployment to test whether we’re making real progress.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a startup’s financial need to survive or how it constrains work on the final model.

r002.rationale: It says deployment can reveal failures and improve data collection, but does not identify a data flywheel that drives progress toward the long-term robotics problem.

r003.rationale: It says long-term research and deployment should reinforce each other, but does not state that both paths may ultimately converge on the same solution.
